I'm designing the Postgres schema for a small invoicing app and want to think the tables through before writing migrations. How should we model customers that belong to more than one workspace?

Use a join table between customers and workspaces with its own created date. That keeps the customer record single while letting each workspace hold its own settings. We can revisit this once we have real traffic numbers. Let me know if you want a short code sample for this part.
What is the cleanest way to number invoices per workspace? We are a team of three, so maintenance cost matters. Please be concrete, I am going to implement this today.

Keep a counter row per workspace and increment it inside the insert transaction. Gaps are acceptable, duplicates are not, so lock the counter row while you increment. We can revisit this once we have real traffic numbers. Let me know if you want a short code sample for this part. A small test around this will catch regressions early.

How should we handle dates and times in the schema? Please be concrete, I am going to implement this today. We can always change it later if needed. We are a team of three, so maintenance cost matters.

Store every instant in UTC with a time zone aware column and convert only at the edges. Due dates are calendar dates, so those can be plain date columns. I would keep the first version boring and well tested. The main thing is to make the choice explicit so the team does not drift.
Do we need a separate table for payment attempts? I want to keep this simple for the first version. Keep in mind we deploy a few times a day.

Yes, record every attempt with its provider response and outcome. The invoice then only stores the final paid state, which keeps it simple to query. Let me know if you want a short code sample for this part. None of this needs to be perfect in the first version. I would add a short comment in the code that explains why it is done this way.

Make it not null, store it lowercased, and add a unique index per workspace. A check constraint for a basic shape is fine, but leave real validation to the app. A small test around this will catch regressions early. I would keep the first version boring and well tested.
How should we handle soft deletes for invoices? We are a team of three, so maintenance cost matters. I have read a few blog posts but they all disagree.

Add a nullable deleted_at column and filter on it in the default queries. A partial index on rows where it is null keeps the common lookups fast. The main thing is to make the choice explicit so the team does not drift.

Should we keep an audit log of changes to invoices? I would rather not add new infrastructure if we can avoid it. Keep in mind we deploy a few times a day. We are a team of three, so maintenance cost matters.

Yes, an append-only table with the actor, the action and a diff of the changed fields is enough. Write to it in the same transaction as the change. The main thing is to make the choice explicit so the team does not drift.
For the primary key type on the users table, let's go with nanoid. I want to keep this simple for the first version.

Good, nanoid for the users table primary key. It gives every row a stable identifier that we can expose in URLs and reference from other tables. I would add a short comment in the code that explains why it is done this way. This also keeps the code easy to read for someone new to the project.
Quick check before I write the migration: which primary key type did we settle on for the users table? Give me the column definition line for it.

response:
```sql
id text PRIMARY KEY, -- NanoID generated by the application
```
